sections.text: These tools explain atomic spectra. The hydrogen atom gives quantised levels and orbitals; selection rules follow from angular momentum and photon spin. The harmonic oscillator has equally spaced levels E_n = (n + 1/2)ℏω. Worked example: an electron in a one-dimensional box of length L = 1.0 nm has E_1 = h²/(8mL²). Using h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and m = 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg gives E_1 = 6.02 × 10⁻²⁰ J, about 0.376 eV.

keyPoints: The time-dependent Schrödinger equation is iℏ ∂ψ/∂t = Ĥψ, and the time-independent form is Ĥψ = Eψ.
Hermitian operators represent observables and have real eigenvalues, and a zero commutator means the observables share eigenstates.
Angular momentum is quantised as L² = ℏ²l(l+1) and Lz = mℏ, with m = −l,...,l.
Electron spin is intrinsic with s = 1/2 and projections m_s = ±1/2.
First-order perturbation theory gives ΔE_n = ⟨n|V̂|n⟩, while the variational energy is an upper bound on the ground-state energy.
For a one-dimensional box, E_n = n²h²/(8mL²), and for L = 1.0 nm the ground state is about 0.376 eV.

en.title: Advanced Statistical Mechanics
en.short: Ensembles, partition functions, quantum statistics, phase transitions and applications.

sections.heading: Ensembles and partition function
sections.text: An ensemble is many copies of a system, each in a possible microscopic state, used to calculate averages. The microcanonical ensemble fixes energy, volume and particle number. The canonical ensemble fixes temperature, volume and number; the grand canonical ensemble fixes temperature, volume and chemical potential μ, the energy change when one particle is added, with particle number free to change. The partition function Z = Σ exp(−βE_i), with β = 1/(k_B T), normalises the canonical probabilities p_i = exp(−βE_i)/Z. It gives the average energy U = −∂ ln Z/∂β and free energy F = −k_B T ln Z. Example: a two-level system with energies 0 and ε has Z = 1 + exp(−βε). At ε = 0.1 eV and T = 300 K, βε ≈ 3.87, so exp(−βε) ≈ 0.021 and U ≈ 0.1 × 0.021 ÷ 1.021 ≈ 0.0021 eV.

sections.heading: Quantum statistics
sections.text: Quantum particles are fermions or bosons. Fermions obey the Pauli exclusion principle, so no two occupy the same single-particle state; their average occupation is n(ε) = 1/[exp(β(ε−μ)) + 1], the Fermi-Dirac distribution. Bosons can share states; their occupation is n(ε) = 1/[exp(β(ε−μ)) − 1], the Bose-Einstein distribution. In the classical limit exp(β(ε−μ)) ≫ 1 both reduce to the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution. These explain blackbody radiation, electrons in metals and Bose-Einstein condensation.

sections.heading: Phase transitions and applications
sections.text: A phase transition is a change in the macroscopic state of a system, marked by an order parameter that is zero in one phase and nonzero in another. First-order transitions involve latent heat; continuous transitions have critical points with power-law behaviour. Landau theory writes the free energy as a series in the order parameter, for example F = a(T−T_c)m² + b m⁴, and minimising it gives m = 0 above T_c and m ≠ 0 below. Statistical mechanics links microscopic models, such as the Ising model of magnetism, to macroscopic properties: heat capacity, magnetisation, conductivity and phase diagrams. The thermodynamic limit, where particle number and volume tend to infinity at fixed density, makes sharp transitions possible.

keyPoints: An ensemble is a probability distribution over microscopic states; the microcanonical, canonical and grand canonical ensembles fix different variables.
The canonical partition function is Z = Σ exp(−βE_i) with β = 1/(k_B T); U = −∂ ln Z/∂β and F = −k_B T ln Z.
Fermions follow Fermi-Dirac statistics n = 1/[exp(β(ε−μ)) + 1]; bosons follow Bose-Einstein statistics n = 1/[exp(β(ε−μ)) − 1].
Classical Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics is the limit exp(β(ε−μ)) ≫ 1.
Phase transitions are described by an order parameter; Landau theory expands the free energy in powers of it.
Statistical mechanics connects microscopic models such as the Ising model to macroscopic properties in the thermodynamic limit.

en.title: Research Methods for a Physics Education Dissertation
en.short: Designs, sampling, instruments, validity, mixed methods, ethics, analysis and dissertation writing.

sections.heading: Designs and sampling
sections.text:
Good designs answer a clear question. Quantitative designs include experimental, quasi-experimental and correlational studies; qualitative designs include case study, phenomenography and action research. A physics education dissertation often compares a teaching method with a control group, or explores learners’ reasoning.

Sampling is the process of choosing participants. Probability sampling (random, stratified, cluster) supports generalisation; non-probability sampling (purposive, convenience, snowball) suits qualitative work. State the population, the sampling frame (the list you sample from) and the sample size, and justify them. In experiments, random assignment reduces bias; in surveys, a representative sample matters.

sections.heading: Instruments and quality
sections.text:
Instrument design turns concepts into measurable items. A questionnaire, interview guide, observation schedule or test needs a blueprint linking each item to a research objective. Validity means the instrument measures what it claims: content validity (coverage of the construct), construct validity (fit with theory) and criterion validity (agreement with an external standard).

Reliability means consistency: test-retest, internal consistency and inter-rater reliability. For example, two coders independently classify 40 answers and agree on 34. Percentage agreement is 34 ÷ 40 = 0.85, or 85%. Report kappa too, because it corrects for chance agreement.

sections.heading: Qualitative, quantitative, mixed
sections.text:
Quantitative methods produce numbers for description and inference. Use means, standard deviations and tests such as t-tests or chi-square when assumptions fit. Qualitative methods produce words and meanings; analyse them with thematic analysis, coding and constant comparison. Trustworthiness replaces reliability and validity: credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability.

Mixed methods combine both, for example a survey followed by interviews (explanatory sequential), or interviews then a questionnaire (exploratory sequential). Explain how the strands integrate.

sections.heading: Ethics, analysis, writing
sections.text:
Ethics require informed consent, voluntary participation, anonymity or confidentiality, protection from harm, and permission from school authorities and an ethics committee.

Data analysis must match the design and question. Write the dissertation as an argument: introduction and problem, literature review, methodology, results, discussion, conclusion and references. Keep the research question, instrument, analysis and claim aligned. Check current institutional guidelines for format and submission.

keyPoints: Align the research question, design, sample, instrument, analysis and conclusion.
Probability sampling supports generalisation; purposive sampling supports depth.
Validity is what an instrument measures; reliability is its consistency.
Percentage agreement = agreed items ÷ total items × 100; for 34 of 40 it is 85%.
Qualitative trustworthiness covers credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability.
Obtain informed consent and ethics approval before collecting data.

en.title: Physics Education Research: Conceptual Understanding and Misconceptions
en.short: Physics education research on misconceptions, conceptual change, representations, inquiry, equity and assessment.

sections.heading: Misconceptions and understanding
sections.text: Physics education research (PER) studies how learners understand physics and why teaching sometimes fails. A misconception, also called an alternative conception, is a stable idea that conflicts with accepted physics, such as “heavier objects always fall faster”. It is not a blank or a careless slip. Learners build such ideas from everyday experience and language. Conceptual understanding means connected, usable knowledge: explaining, predicting, representing and applying ideas, not only recalling definitions. PER uses interviews, concept inventories such as the Force Concept Inventory, which is a multiple-choice test whose wrong options match common misconceptions, and two-tier questions that ask for an answer and a reason.

sections.heading: Conceptual change and representations
sections.text: Conceptual change is restructuring existing ideas, not just adding correct facts. The classic model says change is more likely when a new idea is intelligible, plausible and fruitful, and when the learner is dissatisfied with the old idea. Later research warns that some “misconceptions” are fragments or productive resources. Representations are ways of showing an idea: words, diagrams, graphs, equations, gestures and simulations. Experts move easily between them; novices may treat each as separate. Teaching should make translations explicit, for example from a motion graph to a verbal description.

sections.heading: Inquiry, equity, assessment
sections.text: Inquiry means learning through investigation: asking questions, planning, collecting and interpreting evidence, and explaining. Guided inquiry works better than unstructured discovery for novices. Equity means fair participation, not only equal access. Language, culture, gender, disability and school resources affect who speaks, experiments and succeeds. A deficit view blames students; a resource view asks what they bring. Case: Amina predicts a heavy ball will land first. The teacher asks her to predict, observe two balls of the same size but different masses land together, then explain that gravity gives all objects the same acceleration and that air resistance is why light, spread-out things like paper fall slower. This tests her idea respectfully. Assessment should diagnose understanding before and during teaching. Use formative questions, concept inventories, two-tier items, interviews and representation tasks. Summative assessment should include explanation, prediction, practical reasoning and transfer, not only calculation. Feedback should address the idea, not just the mark. PER findings are context-dependent; check local curricula and your students.

keyPoints: Misconceptions are stable, sensible-to-the-learner ideas that conflict with accepted physics, not simple blanks.
Conceptual understanding means connected knowledge used for explanation, prediction, representation and application.
Conceptual change is more likely when new ideas are intelligible, plausible and fruitful and old ideas are seen as unsatisfactory.
Multiple representations should be translated explicitly, because novices often treat graphs, words and equations as separate.
Guided inquiry and equitable participation help more students test and revise their ideas.
Assessment should diagnose and give feedback on reasoning, not only mark calculations.
